Here are all 7 core mental models broken down visually with real-world case studies.

scenes.headline: Escape Competition Through Uncopyable Skill Stacks
scenes.stat_label: IF SOCIETY CAN TRAIN YOU, IT CAN REPLACE YOU
bullets: Specific knowledge looks like play to you, but work to others
Combine 2-3 skills into a niche few people share
Found at the intersection of childhood curiosity and technical craft
scenes.narration: In 2018, investor and AngelList founder Naval Ravikant published a blueprint that Eric Jorgenson later curated into The Almanack of Naval Ravikant. Its first pillar is Specific Knowledge: the skills you cannot be taught in a standardized classroom. Naval warns that if society can train you by following a checklist, society can eventually replace you with cheaper labor or software. He describes specific knowledge as something that feels like play to you but looks like work to others. Ask yourself what felt like effortless curiosity to you ten years ago that still feels like tedious work to people around you today.
scenes.source: Naval Ravikant, 'How to Get Rich' (2018); Eric Jorgenson, The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020)

scenes.headline: Why Code & Media Beat Labor & Capital for Beginners
scenes.left_body: Labor & Capital: Requires hiring teams, managing egos, or begging investors to say yes
scenes.right_body: Code & Media: Zero gatekeepers, zero marginal cost per extra user or viewer
scenes.narration: Once you identify your specific knowledge, Model Two asks how far a single hour of your judgment can travel. Archimedes famously said, give me a lever long enough and a place to stand, and I will move the earth. For centuries, business relied on two forms of permissioned leverage: labor, meaning people working for you, and capital, meaning money under management. Both require someone else's permission. Naval points to a newer kind: products that cost almost nothing to copy, mainly code and media. You do not need a venture capitalist's signature to write a Python script, publish an educational video essay, or ship a digital template. Recording a video for ten thousand viewers costs the same effort as recording it for ten.
scenes.source: Naval Ravikant, 'How to Get Rich' (2018); Eric Jorgenson, The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020)

scenes.headline: Renting Out Hours Will Never Make You Independent
scenes.stat_label: HOURLY INCOME CAPS OUT - ASSET EQUITY COMPOUNDS
scenes.stat_subtext: Convert active paycheck surplus into businesses, IP, and index ownership
scenes.narration: Model Three is one of the sharpest wake-up calls in modern personal finance: you are not going to gain true financial freedom renting out your time alone. Even high-status salaried professions, like surgeons, corporate attorneys, and senior consultants, face a strict biological cap. When you sleep, take a vacation, or burn out, metered income stops. Real wealth requires owning equity: a piece of a business, intellectual property, software, a media catalog, or diversified productive assets that earn while you are offline. Keep your salary as a launchpad to pay your bills without stress, then systematically channel your surplus hours and savings into assets you actually own.
scenes.source: Naval Ravikant, 'How to Get Rich' (2018); Eric Jorgenson, The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020)

scenes.headline: In the Age of Leverage, Direction Beats Speed
scenes.stat_label: 10% BETTER DECISIONS EARN 10X MORE UNDER LEVERAGE
bullets: Judgment is the skill leverage multiplies
Sprinting fast in the wrong direction multiplies wasted years
Protect an unscheduled calendar so your mind stays clear
scenes.narration: Model Four flips hustle culture upside down. Without leverage, working eighty hours a week produces roughly twice as much as working forty. With leverage, exhausted hours can destroy value because tired brains make sloppy strategic calls. Imagine steering a supertanker: a captain who chooses the right course ninety-five percent of the time is worth far more than one who is right eighty-five percent of the time, even if the second captain works twice as hard. Judgment is the skill leverage multiplies, so protect the time you use to read and think. Treat your calendar like a fortress so your judgment stays sharp.
scenes.source: Illustration based on Naval Ravikant, The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020)

scenes.headline: Play Iterative Games With High-Trust People
scenes.stat_label: 99% OF RETURNS ARRIVE IN THE LATE COMPOUNDING TAIL
scenes.stat_subtext: Switching niches or burning trust resets the exponent back to zero
scenes.narration: Model Five explains why impatience ruins smart builders. Every meaningful reward in life, whether capital, skill mastery, audience trust, or partnerships, comes from compound interest. Yet human beings constantly reset the exponent back to day one by jumping to shiny new trends every ninety days or cutting ethical corners for quick wins. When you work with high-integrity collaborators over a decade, you stop wasting energy on legal friction and office politics. Put accountability behind your work, deliver exactly what you promise, and stay in one compounding lane long enough for the curve to bend upward.
scenes.source: Naval Ravikant, 'How to Get Rich' (2018); Eric Jorgenson, The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020)

scenes.headline: Master First Principles Instead of Memorizing Buzzwords
scenes.left_body: Repeating complex jargon and trendy tactics you cannot explain to a 12-year-old
scenes.right_body: Arithmetic, microeconomics, persuasion, and clear writing from first principles
scenes.narration: How do you actually sharpen judgment? Model Six echoes Nobel physicist Richard Feynman: real thinkers never hide behind complicated jargon. Naval argues it is far better to understand foundational microeconomics, basic probability, human psychology, and clear persuasive writing at a rock-solid level than to memorize advanced buzzwords on shaky ground. Read timeless primary books rather than daily outrage feeds. If you cannot explain why a business model or habit system works on the back of a napkin in plain English, you do not understand it deeply enough to bet your time on it.
scenes.source: Naval Ravikant, 'How to Get Rich' (2018); Eric Jorgenson, The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020)

scenes.headline: Guard Your Time Like It Is Worth $5,000 an Hour
scenes.stat_label: RUTHLESS FILTER FOR DELEGATING & DELETING TRIVIA
bullets: Never spend 3 hours fixing a $40 problem to feel thrifty
Step 1: Audit your Specific Knowledge stack this Sunday
Step 2: Ship 1 piece of Code or Media every week for 52 weeks
scenes.narration: Finally, Model Seven turns philosophy into daily behavior. Long before Naval had real money, he told himself his time was worth five thousand dollars an hour. If outsourcing a task cost less than that, he outsourced it. If fixing a problem saved less than that, he ignored it. Looking back, he says his real rate then was closer to a thousand. You can start at fifty or one hundred dollars an hour today. This Sunday, run a three-step audit: write down the three skills you combine naturally, eliminate one low-value weekly chore, and invest five protected hours shipping one piece of permissionless media or software.
scenes.source: Naval Ravikant, 'Set an Aspirational Hourly Rate', nav.al (2019); The Almanack (2020)
